88	\subsection{Overloading Rules}
89	\label{sec:threerules}
90	
91	Given a class table $\T$, 
92	a set $\D$ of generic function declarations for $\T$, 
93	and a function name $f$, 
94	the set $\Df$ is \emph{valid} 
95	(or is a \emph{valid overloading}) 
96	if it 
97	% VL: quantification over pairs occurs *within* the rules
98	% every pair of declarations in $\Df$ 
99	satisfies the following three rules:
100	
101	% In this section, we describe the rules for valid overloading.
102	% For each function name $f$,
103	% we determine whether a set of overloaded function declarations $\Df$ is valid
104	% by independently considering every pair of declarations in the set.
105	% A set of declarations is a valid overloading 
106	% if every pair of distinct declarations in the set
107	% satisfies the three rules described below with respect to a class
108	% table $\T$, and a set $\Df$ is valid
109	% with respect to $\T$ if every pair of declarations in the set is valid with
110	% respect to $\T$.
111	
112	\begin{description}
113	
114	\item[No Duplicates Rule]
115	For every $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$, 
116	if $d_1 \ms d_2$ and $d_2 \ms d_1$ 
117	%then $d_1$ and $d_2$ denote the same declaration. 
118	then $d_1 = d_2$.
119	
120	\item[Meet Rule]
121	For every $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$,
122	there exists a declaration $d_0 \in \Df$ (possibly $d_1$ or $d_2$) 
123	such that,
124	% for every type $T \in \T$, $d_0$ is applicable to $T$ 
125	% if and only if both $d_1$ and $d_2$ are applicable to $T$.
126	$d_0 \ms d_1$ and $d_0 \ms d_2$ 
127	and $d_0$ is applicable to any type $T \in \T$ 
128	to which both $d_1$ and $d_2$ are applicable.
129	
130	\item[Return Type Rule]
131	For every $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$ with $d_1 \ms d_2$,
132	and every type $T \not\equiv \Bottom$ such that $d_1 \in \Df(T)$,
133	% (and thus $d_2 \in \Df(T)$),
134	if an instance $\decl{f}{S_2}{T_2}$ of $d_2$ is applicable to $T$,
135	then there is an instance \decl{f}{S_1}{T_1} of $d_1$
136	that is applicable to $T$ with \mbox{$T_1 <: T_2$}.
137	
138	\end{description}
139	
140	The No Duplicates Rule forbids distinct declarations from being equally specific 
141	(i.e., each more specific than the other).
142	
143	The Meet Rule requires every pair of declarations 
144	to have a \emph{disambiguating declaration}, 
145	which is more specific than both 
146	and applicable whenever both are applicable.
147	(If one of the pair is more specific than the other, 
148	then it is the disambiguating declaration.)
149	
150	The Return Type Rules guarantees that
151	whenever the type checker might have used an instance of a declaration $d_2$ 
152	to check a program,
153	and then a more specific declaration $d_1$ is selected by dynamic dispatch,
154	then there is some instance of $d_1$ that is applicable to the argument 
155	and whose return type is a subtype 
156	of the return type of the instance of $d_2$ 
157	the type checker used, 
158	which is necessary for type preservation, 
159	as discussed above.
160	
161	Since $\Bottom$ is well-formed, 
162	% with respect to any class table, 
163	and tuple types with different numbers of arguments 
164	have no common subtype other than \Bottom,
165	the Meet Rule requires that 
166	an overloaded function with declarations that take different numbers of arguments 
167	have a declaration applicable only to \Bottom.
168	Such a declaration would never be applied 
169	(because no value belongs to \Bottom), 
170	and it cannot be written in Fortress 
171	(because \Bottom\ is not first-class).
172	To avoid this technicality, 
173	we implicitly augment every set $\Df$ 
174	with a declaration $\decl{f}{\Bottom}{\Bottom}$.
175	This declaration is strictly more specific 
176	than any declaration that a programmer can write,
177	and its return type is a subtype of every type, 
178	so it trivially satisfies all three rules 
179	when checked with any other declaration in $\Df$.
180	
181	This technicality raises the following question:
182	Must the Meet Rule hold for every $T \in \T$?
183	Could we not, for example, 
184	have excluded \Bottom\ from consideration, 
185	as in the Return Type Rule, 
186	and avoided the technicality?
187	If so, 
188	for which types is it necessary that the Meet Rule hold?
189	The answer is,
190	we must check the Meet Rule for a type $T \in \T$ 
191	to which both $d_1$ and $d_2$ are applicable
192	if there could be a value of type $T$ 
193	such that for any type $T' \in \T$ 
194	to which the value belongs, $T \subtypeof T'$.
195	In other words, 
196	we must check it for all ````leaf'' types.
197	Thus, if we did not require extensibility, 
198	we can check the Meet Rule only for those types that are ilks of values.
199	However, 
200	because we require extensibility, 
201	and we support multiple inheritance,
202	we use intersection types instead.

206	\subsection{Mechanically Checking the Rules}
207	With our interpretations of applicability and specificity into existential
208	subtyping, we now describe the process of checking the validity of a set of 
209	overloaded declarations $\Df$ according to the rules in
210	Section~\ref{sec:rules}.
211	
212	We can check the No Duplicates Rule by verifying that for every pair of distinct function
213	declarations $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$ either $d_1 \not \ms d_2$ or $d_1 \not \ms d_2$. 
214	
215	The Meet Rule requires that every pair of declarations $d_1, d_2 \in \Df$ 
216	has a meet in $\Df$. 
217	Because the more specific relation on function declarations 
218	corresponds to the subtyping relation on the (existential) domain types,
219	we just need to find a declaration $d_0 \in \Df$ 
220	whose domain type $dom(d_0)$ 
221	is equivalent to the meet (under $\le$) 
222	of the existential types $\dom(d_1)$ and $\dom(d_2)$.
223	Figure~\ref{fig:meet} shows how to compute the meet of two existential types.
224	
225	\begin{lemma}\label{lem:meet}
226	$\delta_1 \meet \delta_2$ (as defined in Figure~\ref{fig:meet}) 
227	is the meet of $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ under $\le$.
228	\end{lemma}
229	\begin{proof}
230	First we show that $\delta_1 \meet \delta_2$ is the meet of $\delta_1$ and $\delta_2$ under $\leinner$. That $\delta_1 \meet \delta_2 \leinner \delta_1$ and $\delta_1 \meet \delta_2 \leinner \delta_2$ is obvious.
231	For any $\delta_0$, if $\bar{U}$ and $\bar{V}$ are instantiations that prove
232	$\delta_0 \leinner \delta_1$ and $\delta_0 \leinner \delta_2$, respectively,
233	then we can use the instantiation $\bar{U},\bar{V}$ to prove that $\delta_0 \le \delta_1 \meet \delta_2$.
234	
235	Now we show that the meet under $\leinner$ is also the meet under $\le$. Suppose that $\delta_0 \le \delta_1$, $\delta_0 \le \delta_1$,
236	and $\jtred{\delta_0}{\delta'_0}$. A little work lets us deduce that $\delta'_0 \leinner \delta_1 \meet \delta_2$ and hence $\delta_0 \le \delta_1 \meet \delta_2$.
237	The fact that $\delta_1 \meet \delta_2 \le \delta_1$ and $\delta_1 \meet \delta_2 \le \delta_2$ follows from the fact that $\leinner$ implies $\le$.
238	\end{proof}
239	
240	We can check the Return Type Rule using the subtype relation on universal types.
241	\begin{theorem}
242	Let $d_1 = \hdeclg{f}{\Delta_1}{S_1}{T_1}$ and $d_2 = \hdeclg{f}{\Delta_2}{S_2}{T_2}$ be declarations
243	in $\Df$ with $d_1 \ms d_2$. 
244	They satisfy the Return Type Rule if $\arrow(d_1)$ is a subtype of
245	the arrow type $\sigma_{\wedge} = \forall\ob{\Delta_1, \Delta_2}(S_1 \cap S_2) \rightarrow T_2$.
246	\end{theorem}
247	
248	\begin{proof}
249	Let $d_{\wedge} = f\ob{\Delta_1, \Delta_2} S_1 \cap S_2 : T_2$, 
250	so $\arrow(d_{\wedge}) = \sigma_{\wedge}$. 
251	Note that $d_{\wedge}$ and $d_1$ are equally specific and 
252	that $d_{\wedge}$ and $d_2$ satisfy the Return Type Rule. 
253	Because $\arrow(d_1) \le \sigma_{\wedge}$,
254	for every instance $\arrowtype{U}{V}$ of $\sigma_{\wedge}$ with $U \not \equiv \Bottom$,
255	we can find an instance $\arrowtype{U_1}{V_1}$ of $\arrow(d_1)$ 
256	with $U \subtypeof U_1$ and $V_1 \subtypeof V$. 
257	Thus, the pair $d_1$ and $d_2$ satisfy the Return Type Rule because the pair $d_{\wedge}$, $d_2$ does.
258	\end{proof}

260	## One replacement premise
261	
262	Write $P\le Q$ for subtyping and $P<Q$ for strict subtyping. Let $v$ be the
263	argument value (a tuple for multiple arguments), $X$ its ilk, and $A$ its
264	static type. Membership $v\in P$ entails $X\le P$; type soundness gives
265	$X\le A$.
266	
267	Replace the exact-meet requirement for overlapping incomparable domains
268	$P,Q$ by **Cover-Meet**: there are visible concrete declarations with domains
269	$C_1,\ldots,C_n$ such that
270	
271	$$
272	C_i\le P,\quad C_i\le Q,\qquad
273	v\in P\cap Q\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists i:\ v\in C_i .
274	$$
275	
276	The last condition quantifies every permitted value, not merely the current
277	call or objects observed in a test. Require Cover-Meet for every incomparable
278	overlapping pair in the family, including pairs among the covering
279	declarations. An empty overlap needs no resolving declaration.
280	
281	This is a separate coverage judgement. It does **not** assert the nominal
282	subtyping identity $P\cap Q=\bigcup_i C_i$.

378	Clause expansion is a finite symbolic justification from declared closed

380	arguments correctly, prove each resolving domain below both competitors,

107	## 5. The boundaries the rung keeps
108	
109	- **The shared analyzer.** `TypeAnalyzer.scala` is not in the diff: `subtype`, `meet`, `equivalent`, `normConjunct` and the normalizer are the base's. `coversOverlap` has one caller, `coverageRule` (`grep -rn coversOverlap ProjectFortress/src` gives the definition and that call). A coverage result is a boolean the overloading check reads and nothing else; no subtype, assignment or equivalence verdict can move through it. `SkBetweenAssign` keeps its refusal, "Right-hand side has type G[\ZZ32\], but declared type is V", and so does `OwnClauseBetween` ("Right-hand side has type M, but declared type is V"), base and edit alike.
110	- **Astra's boundary.** The intersection typing applies only in a family without static parameters (`groundFamily`, `Functionals.scala:683`), so never to a generic declaration that needs a run-time instantiation; `G[\ZZ32\]` is an instantiated argument type and in the ground case. The scope is narrower than the boundary, which excludes only generic declarations that may run: a family with a generic declaration that cannot apply to the argument keeps the head of a sort (section 14, D6).
111	- **Coercion.** A tie that involves a coercion the call needs or a promoted candidate keeps batch N's rules; rung I's tie tests keep their verdicts (section 6).
112	- **The Return Type Rule is a premise.** `XXXCoverageReturnBad` is refused on it:

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
source "$(dirname "$0")/../../../experiment/env.sh"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
